qs.q: A patient with a chronic granulomatous disease develops a fungal infection that forms granulomas. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is most likely involved?
qs.e: Granuloma formation is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to intracellular fungi.

qs.q: In a patient with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), neutrophils fail to kill ingested bacteria. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
o: NADPH oxidase complex in the phagosomal membrane
Myeloperoxidase within the primary azurophilic granules
Inducible nitric oxide synthase in the macrophage cytoplasm
Cyclooxygenase-2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum
qs.e: CGD results from inherited deficiencies in components of NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase), which is essential for the respiratory burst that generates superoxide (O2•) and subsequent reactive oxygen species. This enzyme complex normally assembles rapidly when neutrophils phagocytose bacteria - cytosolic components translocate to the phagosomal membrane to form the active enzyme. qs.q: Which cellular process is impaired in patients with chronic granulomatous disease?
qs.e: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defects in NADPH oxidase, which is required for the respiratory burst that generates superoxide (O2•−) in leukocytes. This impairs their ability to kill phagocytosed microbes, leading to recurrent infections. ## SECTION 5: OTHER MECHANISMS OF CELL DEATH
